ai_answer: The Supreme Court has held that Article 21 protects the right to life and personal liberty as a fundamental right that is not limited to a single repository.  In *Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.* the Court emphasized that Article 21 is the sole repository of the right to life and personal liberty, but it is not the only source of such rights, and that the right is broad and includes various unenumerated liberties.  In *Unni Krishnan [Not Verified] * the Court clarified that the expression ‘personal liberty’ is comprehensive, encompassing privacy, dignity, and the freedom to move, and that these attributes are part of the right to life and personal liberty.  In *People’[Not Verified] * the Court reiterated that personal liberty is of the widest amplitude and that several unenumerated rights, such as the right to privacy and the right to go abroad, fall within Article 21.  Thus, Article 21 protects a wide array of rights, including the right to life, personal liberty, privacy, dignity, and freedom of movement, and the Court has repeatedly affirmed that these rights are fundamental and cannot be deprived without lawful authority.

question: freedom of speech and reasonable restrictions under Article 19
citations: KAUSHAL KISHOR versus STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ORS. [2023] 8 S.C.R. 581 (2023)
LIFE INSURANCE CORPN. OF INDIA AND ORS. ETC. versus PROF. MANUBHAI D. SHAH ETC. ETC. [1992] 3 S.C.R. 595 (1992)

top_3_cases.title: KAUSHAL KISHOR versus STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ORS.
LIFE INSURANCE CORPN. OF INDIA AND ORS. ETC. versus PROF. MANUBHAI D. SHAH ETC. ETC.
SHREYA SINGHAL versus UNION OF INDIA

ai_answer: The Supreme Court has held that Article 19(1)(a) does not confer an absolute right to freedom of speech and expression; it is subject to reasonable restrictions enumerated in Article 19(2).  The Court has repeatedly emphasized that the right is accompanied by duties towards fellow citizens and society, and that speech which is hate speech, defamatory, or otherwise contrary to the content of Article 19(1)(a) may be restrained.  Restrictions must be made only on the grounds listed in Article 19(2) and must be reasonable, proportionate and necessary to protect the interests of the state, community or individual rights.  The Court has also clarified that the right must be exercised so as not to conflict with the rights of others or with the paramount interests of the state.
